utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the registry staff and the Prosecution and Defence counsels. Let us take up our work where we left off, and I think it was Mr. Jovanovic's turn. Please proceed, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of the accused Mladjo Radic calls Witness Nebojsa Jokic to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The order of witnesses which we were given indicates that today's witness would -- the first one, actually, would have been yesterday's witness, Drazenko -- or I'm sorry, Ranko Radic, and today's witness is supposed to be the son of Mladjo Radic, Drazenko Radic. So we have -- this is completely askew in terms of the order of witnesses that we've been presented and for which we have prepared. I mean, we can go forward, but I'd like the Court to understand that this is a complete deviation from the third set of witness schedules that we've been provided by the Radic Defence team. Yesterday's witness was to have been Drazenko Radic, followed by Ranko Radic. I did raise this with the Court, indicating we were prepared to go ahead. We had done, certainly, our work, but this is simply an impossible situation for us. We don't know which schedule they intend to follow even when new ones are provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for today we have two remaining witnesses, so the only change was that yesterday we heard Ranko Radic, and Drazenko Radic will be there today. But Mr. Jokic is the only one -- only remaining witness for this week, according to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, you have the two witnesses here with you today, ready and waiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, which witness would you like to testify first?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: According to the schedule, the first witness should be - excuse me, Your Honour - Drazenko Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want Drazenko Radic. Can you have that witness brought in today, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a pity that, Ms. Susan Somers, that you weren't here from the beginning, but anyway, let us proceed. It is a little complicated. If there are two witnesses for today, Ms. Susan Somers, I don't think there ought to be a problem, but anyway, let us comply with your wishes. We shall comply with your wishes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I shall begin my examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Witness, would you tell the court your name and surname to start off with?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: My name is Drazenko Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And your father's name?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Mladjo Bosiljka. I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: The 25th of June, 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What are you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your religion?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us try and make pauses between question and answer. Thank you. What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I am a food technologist, but I work as a policeman and have completed all the training courses necessary to become a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should now like to ask the usher to show the witness Defence Exhibit D93 and D93A. Witness Drazenko, take a look at that piece of paper, please, and I shall be asking you some questions about it later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I think it is Exhibit D9/3, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is the number we received from the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is for purposes of the record, so it is not Exhibit D93, it is in fact D9/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour. Yes, it seems to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, just to clear up matters for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Drazenko, have you had a look at that diagram?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court everything you know about that document, but slowly and approach the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: This is a list for the Police Department of Omarska for the May, June, July, August period, 1992, from which we can see on what day and at what time my father was on duty. It is the duty roster, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who gave you this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: The books, the registration books, roster, was to be found in the present Omarska Police Department, and I got it in Prijedor talking to the chief of the centre there. One of the employees took this to be photocopied so I don't know what comes before and what comes after, but he photocopied just the section referring to my father. On the other side is the stamp of the Central Security Station and the chief made an addendum, an additional document, explaining what this particular document was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know where that log or roster or register was taken -- is located, where you took this from?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Now, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who did you give this document to, the document that you obtained?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I handed over the document to the former Defence counsel. It was sometime in May, 1998. That is, the counsel's name was Veljko Guberina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you received this document, was anybody else present when Dzenadija handed you the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I had a conversation with him in his office in the morning and on that same day, I think it was the 12th of May, 1998, in my police station, a working meeting was held for him to come, who had taken over the function of chief, and for him to -- and he handed over this envelope with the document in the Prijedor 2 Police Station in the presence of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you yourself are a policeman can you see from that piece of paper the duty roster and when your father was on duty, in fact, when he performed his duties, according to that roster?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the duty roster that every police station must have, and this is the way that data is kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And from the document, you can see his shifts, is that correct, when he was on duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: On the screen, I don't know what month it was, but I see that he worked for three or four days, eight hours, and then as I recall in June, they worked 12 hours one day and then were off for 24 hours. So that the rhythm there was 12, 24, 12 hours, 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to address a matter to the Chamber. The document that we have labelled D9/3 is handwritten not typed. It looks nothing like the document which is on the screen. And I am not clear at all what document is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila, your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot see. All I can see is what is on the screen. It is the document that I handed in to the Prosecution and that the Prosecution examined when Mr. Niemann was in your place. If you will recall, Mr. Niemann took the document, examined it and returned it. And that is the same document which I myself obtained from the former Defence counsel so that my knowledge is equal to that of Ms. Somers' knowledge about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, what document is document D9/3, in fact? What document is that? Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO. I will get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Ah, the lower one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Fila, one moment, please. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original document was handed over, and the original is handwritten. What Ms. Somers can see on the screen is the translation, and of course the translation is typed out on a typewriter. Now, I am going to ask the witness to have a look at the original. So that is the difference. The typewritten copy is the translation and the original is the one below. It is handwritten. Now you have them both, both documents on the screen. The top one is the translation, the bottom one is the handwritten original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And what is the number of the original document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the same document, D9/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, the manuscript, what is the number of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The document which I have which reflects --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. The document in my possession that is handwritten, Your Honours, is D9/3, and there is a typed edition that is 3A. My understanding was they were looking at 3 and they didn't have 3A on the ELMO to us. So I just need to know what we're looking at. It's terribly confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D9/3 is the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I myself saw was that we had a document number D9/3, and there was another document D9/3A, and that is the translation, and that is where the difference lies, the only difference. Therefore, the original is the handwritten document and the other is the translation. So where is the problem, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The reference to 3, Your Honour, is -- we were following 3, which is handwritten, and it was not appearing on the ELMO at all, a typed one, and we weren't sure what the story was, so -- they were reading from. It's okay. It's clear now. I appreciate your clearing it up. Thank you for helping us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the version that is on the ELMO is the translation of the original version, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The original is what we were trying to get at, and that was hidden on the bottom of the ELMO, and we were looking at that document, Your Honour. Thank you very much. You've cleared it up for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at the original that you received in the envelope from Dzenadija and tell us what you see on the original document.

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: The copy is not a very good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking you about the original.

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I can't quite see it very well, but in the first part, after the line, is the first 15 days of the month, and the second part is the last 15 days of the month. And the date is to be found at the top of the book, top of the log or roster, and we go downwards. Now, I can't see the month, but he worked on the 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th and was off on the 7th. Or if we look at the second column, we can see, next to the dark line, the 16th, 17th, and 18th my father was on duty. I can't see the time. The 19th he was off and he worked again on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I wish to learn from you is the following: Does that mean that on the day this was done, the book, the roster, the register, the log, existed?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How can you explain the fact that the Prosecution looked for that roster but couldn't find it? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't explain that. Perhaps it would be up to the centre, our centre, to explain that, because they provided me with the original roster.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at the upper section, and it says something there. It says policajac, does it not, policeman? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Policeman, an ordinary policeman on the beat, a foot policeman, somebody doing the classical type of police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that is the duty roster of an ordinary policeman on the beat?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You can return the document now. We don't need it any longer. Finally, Mr. Radic, you are the son of Mladjo Radic. Could you, in a few words, explain to us who are your family members now? Who do you have living in your family now?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor there is my mother and three sons. My mother and three sons now live in Prijedor. I am the eldest son.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do any of you work?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I am the only person that is employed. My mother is employed too but has not been working since the war began, nor does she receive any remuneration.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How high is your salary, if I may ask an industry question?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: My salary is 320 German marks and I have 80 marks' worth of hot meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that means that the four of you live on the basis of those 400 German marks?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tell us, please: What kind of father was your father, Mladjo Radic? What was your upbringing? How did he bring you up? What were the relationships in your family?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Our family was an average worker's family. He grew up in a large family. His mother came from a large family. And we children grew up in a family where our parents worked. We went to school, we were a modest family, we did what -- we worked at school. They went about their own business. We helped them do the agricultural work, because we have a small plot of land. But generally he brought us up to be good people, never to do any ill to others, and I hope we have succeeded in that, but it is up to others to judge this, of course. It is not up to me to talk about myself. But as far as I am able to say, we have always upheld the family dignity and have always saved face, if I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fila. Would any of the other Defence counsel like to ask any questions? I see Mr. Simic -- Mr. Nikolic -- Mr. Simic would not. Mr. Nikolic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have just one question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radic. You said, in answer to a question from Mr. Fila, that you are a policeman today.

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And I quote your words. You said that you completed all the courses, training courses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Had you not completed those courses, would you be able to become a policeman, had you not graduated from those courses?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I said all courses, and today --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I'm just asking you: Had you not completed those training courses, the courses that you did complete, could you become a policeman without those policemen [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could be a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions from any of the other Defence counsel? No. Thank you. Ms. Susan Somers, your witness for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the document which you just were asked about that was on the ELMO, D9/3, the original, I would ask you to take a look at that again for a moment, please, in the original. The original, please. Thank you very much. You were asked by Mr. Fila to take a look at the upper section, and you gave a term in Serbo-Croat that was policajac; correct? You said policajac.

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, tell me: Where is that shown? I don't see that word on here at all. I see a different word. I see milicioner. Where did you come up with the term policajac, and is there a difference in your mind?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. In the former Yugoslavia, we used to say milicioner for policeman. Today we use the word policajac for policeman. That's the only difference. But it's the same person, the same job, the same thing, which used to be known as milicioner as policeman, and now policeman is policajac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you're absolutely sure about that, a hundred per cent?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Absolutely 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you become a police officer, exactly?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I began working on the 1st of April, 1997. That was my first working day in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Have you always worked in the Prijedor police department? Where do you work? Which department are you working in?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Since the beginning, that is to say, the 1st of April, 1997, I worked in the police station Prijedor 2, and sometime around the new year I was transferred to the security centre and the intervention team.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1997 who was the chief of Prijedor 2 Police Station, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Then and now, Mr. Ranko Jakovljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your father was working under Simo Drljaca. Do you know from when to when he was working under Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Drljaca is the chief of the centre. As far as I remember, he was there in the first years of the war. I was 16 or 17 at the time so I can't give you that information. I don't know. But when I came to the police force, that man was no longer there. That is to say he did not have a position of leadership there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You entered the police force at a time when your father was already under indictment. You knew that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Only from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The rest of the police department knew your father was under indictment as well, did it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: They probably knew only from the media. You couldn't learn anything concrete. It wasn't accessible, any concrete information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did your father tell you that Simo Drljaca helped him falsify documents to allow him to stay as a police officer after he was indicted?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know that your father was not permitted to be a police officer after he was indicted?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Maybe I know that now because I have graduated from all the international courses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1997, you were working as a police officer because, as you just told us, you had been trained as a police officer. Were you not told that if you are charged with a crime, you cannot be, during that period of time, a police officer, or is that missing from Yugoslav law?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I began working on the 1st of April, 1997. And the course for the police force organised by the MUP of Republika Srpska I graduated from, from the 20th of June to the 20th of October, 1998, so perhaps on the 30th of February or 28th or 9th of February, whether it was a leap year or not, or March, I was a civilian, and on the 1st of April I put on the uniform. I completed the course only in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your father was arrested in February, is that correct, of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were a police officer at the time of his arrest, or you had completed your training and were on the road to becoming a police officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. In 1998, October, I finished the police course and he was arrested on the 8th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Explain, please, what you began working on on the 1st of April, 1997?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I remember my first working day, as anybody else would. I reported to the police station, to the commander there. He looked at the duty roster and told me to go to the Bijelo Dugme restaurant where a patrol of two policemen waited for me, and I spent the whole day on patrol with those two policemen. And so the next few days, I would change patrols but that's the work I did. So I was on the beat with the patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you were acting in capacity of, at the very least, a police officer in training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you were effectively working as a police officer in training in the same department or region that your father was working in as a police officer without a right to be a police officer. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: On the territory of the same Security Service Centre but they are different police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you had been charged with violations of the laws of war, among other crimes against -- international humanitarian law crimes, would you have been allowed to retain your police-officer-in-training status and become certified by IPTF? They would ask you, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I would just like to explain one thing. A formal indictment was never received by my father, so all the stories came from the media. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Under normal circumstances, we know that nobody can work if he is a suspect in a crime of some kind. But there was -- he never received an official request to report to the court or anything like that. And I should like to mention that they were the post-war years and there was a lot of problems on the -- of security and that he -- if he gave himself up, we as a family would have had problems in those post-war years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You are a police officer. What is your understanding of your obligations to uphold the law? Please explain that.

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Every policeman must be honourable -- work honourably and perform his duties professionally and uphold the law, and adhere to the law and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you as a police officer believe that your personal interest takes precedence over the law?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. Every policeman who is an honourable policeman has the law first and the constitution, and afterwards -- that is to say, there are no personal interests in that service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you on duty the day your father was arrested?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about these documents which you were explaining something about. There was a reference made during your examination in chief to the Prosecutor seeking documents. Tell me, please, were you able, just to walk in to the Prijedor police department and say, "I want these documents about a person's record, not my own, another person's record," and receive them? Was that all it took?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. Like any other citizen, I went -- I asked for an interview with the chief, and I asked -- I asked for a meeting with him in the next day or two, and that person received me. We talked, and I asked him for the document and we saw whether this was -- we discussed whether this was possible -- I asked whether that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you telling us that it is in the exclusive discretion of the chief as to whether or not a document is given out or copied? Is that what you're telling us the law is?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: The gentleman who had given me certain documents gave me the documents which are allowed to be presented. And all the documents which came through were requested by the lawyers' office. If that document should not have been available to me because there was another interested party or another vested interest, then I certainly did not receive it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you telling me that if the Office of the Prosecutor representative walks in to Marko Dzenadija and says, "I want a copy of the record of Drazenko Radic for a certain day," we can just get it? Is that your position? Just walk in and get it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, he -- you would probably get it. I followed a certain procedure. I requested a certain document and received what I could. I certainly did not receive all that I requested. I don't know whether those documents which I did not receive and have requested exist at all but all I know is that I did not receive them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you give this document to Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He never gave that document to Mr. Fila but to Mr. Veljko Guberina, and I received them from Mr. Guberina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Fila, you will have the opportunity to ask your additional questions. You cannot contest the witness's answers, past or future.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has answered. You can look at the transcript, and he said that the document -- that he gave the documents to Mr. Veljko Guberina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Mr. Fila, but his answers have to be coherent. Ms. Somers, please mind the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you give the documents to whatever Defence lawyer asked you to get them?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I said I got it on the 12th of May, 1998, and on the same day I handed it to a lawyer from the office of Mr. Veljko Guberina, lawyer Nenad Vukasovic who was in the service of Mr. Guberina, who worked for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Fila when he became your father's lawyer that you had given documents over to this individual, and that particular document among them?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed all the documents which the previous team had given to the then Defence counsel and I don't think that anything was missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did your father himself ask you to get that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. The only thing that my father requested from me personally was when the previous lawyer was visiting him, was a list of people whom he had helped, but my father didn't insist even on that. All that was in question was a list of people who -- whom he had helped. And I needed it for my future work anyway and I succeeded in procuring it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Why did you need it for your future work?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. -- the Defence counsel from the previous office requested it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You said your future work. Are you acting as an investigator for your father's Defence case?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. It is -- I derive a moral satisfaction from attempting to help my father, who is a suspect here, and I'm trying to help as much as I can. It is my own personal wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you using your position as a police officer to get information that you are not entitled to get?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. All that I have done I did in my free time. I never mentioned that I was a police officer. If I interviewed any witnesses, potential or otherwise, I never mentioned that in my conversations with them. I never mentioned that I was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What witnesses did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, how much time do you think you need to finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I have three more minutes, if I may? Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute only.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the names of the witnesses you've interviewed.

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I was hoping you would ask that. Last night, out of my memory, I wrote a list, and if you allow it, it's in my jacket. I could read it out in a closed session because most of those people thanked my father for helping them but for the sake of their own personal safety, they do not dare come here and testify. I have this list with me but I wouldn't like to read it in public.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And over what period of time did you interview these witnesses, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Since his arrest until a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does Mr. Fila have a copy of these documents, the lists?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. It's a list I wrote for myself last night. I have statements from some of those people. Mr. Fila, I believe, has their statements, the statements of several of them, but those people told me openly that they dare not come here and testify, for reasons of their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your parents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, please finish. Please finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm. The record reflects the fact that your parents are Mladjo and Bosiljka. You have how many brothers, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Two brothers, Marko [as interpreted] and Milos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Last question. When you were at home, were you living at home while your dad was serving in Omarska? Were you living at home with your parents?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, finish; otherwise I will take the floor away from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You are abusing your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies. Thank you very much, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the name which is on the transcript is Marko, and it's actually Darko. It should be corrected. As for additional questions, I don't have any, but if the Trial Chamber requires it, the list that was mentioned can be brought and presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, do you have any additional questions? Mr. Judge Riad? Judge Wald?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, this is just about the document D9/3. What was on the ELMO -- and the only thing that I was able to see was the handwritten version of the roster for some month, and I think you said you couldn't tell by looking at that which month that was; is that right? The one that was shown, that you couldn't tell what month that was. Did I hear you right or ... Yes. All I'm trying to understand now is the document that you got originally from the Public Security Centre says in the statement that it's the duty rosters for May, June, July, and August. So were there other rosters? And maybe they're in the exhibit that I don't have before me. I'm just trying to clarify now what it is that we have before us. Are there other documents like the one we saw on the ELMO for other months, or do you know? If you don't ...

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I wish to clarify the principles along which these duty rosters are drafted. The worker who comes to work in the morning receives a list from yesterday, and he writes in hand who was on duty, where, the previous day. And the log goes from January, a list of all the workers is made for one month, then one sheet is left empty and another month -- the log for another month is started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's a very simple question that I just want to get straight. Is what we saw on the ELMO, D9/3, is that the only duty roster that you got from Mr. Dzenadija and handed over to the counsel, or are there other ones for other months, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, when they were doing the photocopying for May, June, July, and August, that was in the middle of this log, and earlier on in that log and after that there are probably other months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And you think or you -- if it's true that you think that there were other months' rosters that were handed over by you to the counsel, or do you know? I'm just trying to figure out if that's the only piece of paper we have on rosters or whether, to your knowledge, there were other pieces of paper, rosters for other months, such as is suggested by the statement, though not conclusively, that you handed over to the Defence counsel, if you know. Was that the only piece of paper you know about or were there others like that that you think or know you handed over to Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: You mean as far as duty rosters are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's all I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: There are duty rosters for the months that I have mentioned, and there is a cover letter written by Mr. Dzenadija, registered under number 14198, where it says: "For purposes of defence of Mladjo Radic," and so on and so forth, "we hereby submit an extract from the duty roster, a log book." That's all I have seen, all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And that's what you handed over to the old Defence counsel, the one that preceded Mr. Fila; right? You handed all that that you just talked about over to the prior Defence counsel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. Mr. Radic, I myself have a question for you. Do you remember the exact words you have used when talking to the director of the centre when you were asking for this document? What exactly did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact words, but I said that I need any document that could help me. He told me that I have to check in the local police department in Omarska. That document was there. I reported to the commander. I think his deputy was on duty then. He showed me that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said any document that could help you. You said that was what you told the director. Did you say, "Give me any document which could be helpful to me," or did you have in mind, already then, that document, this particular one?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: I was talking primarily about duty rosters. That was my primary interest because that was what the Defence counsel had requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why duty rosters?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: That was what the Defence counsel requested. He was with me in the office that day. And when the chief got the copies, he handed them to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And when the chief was giving you the documents, the Defence counsel was present?

utterances.speaker: DRAZENKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. As I said, I was at a meeting in my own police station. The Defence counsel had come to -- sorry. The chief had come to meet the people, because he took over that duty just a month or so before. He wanted to meet everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Radic. Thank you for having come. I think it was a pleasure. We wish you a safe journey home. I see Mr. Fila is on his feet. Shall I give you the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wished, in connection with Judge Wald's question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to wait for the interpretation to finish. Mr. Fila, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honours would look at document D9/3, on the back of the original you would find the answer to the question put by Judge Wald. There is the original stamp and the signature of Mr. Dzenadija. It was not shown on our computer screens. It's on the back of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. I would like the usher to see this witness out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, I believe we no longer have a problem with the sequence of witnesses. In any case, let me just make a remark. Ms. Somers, Mr. Waidyaratne is on your side. He can tell you all the problems we've had in this trial with changes of sequences, changes of lists on both -- on the part of both sides. Perhaps before you make another objection you should ask Mr. Waidyaratne for advice. You have not been here since the beginning. I understand that. As I told you yesterday, I am trying and the Trial Chamber is trying to maintain a balance between the parties. I don't know if ultimately I should make a report so that both parties understand the reaction of this Trial Chamber, because there have been many incidents indeed. And I understand that we are here almost at the end of the trial. We have seen Mr. Niemann, Ms. Hollis, Mr. Keegan, then again Ms. Hollis, and now you as the Prosecutor in charge of this trial. But we have to bring this trial to an end. We have great difficulties in doing so. And I want to tell you another thing. This Chamber knows well the state of the affairs where the Prosecutor cannot continue the case because they want to change the team. The Prosecution team is constantly changing, without any consideration. I must say this also in public, because you also have to understand the difficulties we are encountering in conducting this trial. Please bear in mind these issues. Today we have only two witnesses. That means that you have been prepared for both of them, so it makes no sense to object; at least, that is my opinion. I would like to ask Mr. Simic [sic] for some more patience. I am reacting pedagogically, so to speak, to try to make you see that it's useless to make such objections. We must bear in mind that we have to facilitate the work of others. It's always a good idea. We will now continue. I see that you wish to respond. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and I want to thank you. I'll only take one minute. I do not want to cut into counsel's time but I want to make it clear to the Chamber that I am painfully aware of the difficulties that this Chamber has had in effectively having a steady staff, and as I indicated when I was assigned to this case, that barring my death, I hope to finish this case timely and very expeditiously in terms of procedure. My concern, so the Chamber knows, is that the order is important for us. I need to release a member of my staff but more importantly, as we have spent, perhaps with -- more than any other Defence team, we have spent a lot of time, including meetings just recently, with the Radic Defence team and we were handed these documents. We had face-to-face meetings which I think the Chamber has encouraged us to do. We are trying to puts issues that don't need to waste the time of the Chamber to bed outside of the courtroom. And my concern is that having had a number of meetings, phone calls and letters - and I'm sure that my learned opponents would agree with this - the change was worked on us really with surprise and the disappointment I think is perhaps what the Chamber needs to know. I want to see things finish as well. We all have next cases to move on to and other things to do. And should there have been any inconvenience or misunderstanding, we apologise. The Prosecution is committed to seeing this case through fairly and effectively and efficiently. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Jovanovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In response to what my learned colleague said, I wish to say there has been only one minor change on the whole, instead of Drazenko Radic who was supposed to testify yesterday, Radko Radic came yesterday. That was the only change. And I would now like to invite in witness Nebojsa Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming. You are going to be answering questions posed to you by Mr. Jovanovic first. Your witness, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Nebojsa Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: The 8th of June, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I'm a driver and a car mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work, in which company?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm working in the Ljubija mine at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you work in a different company before that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Before that, I worked in AutoTransport Prijedor for about nine or ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, could you please pause after my question in order for the interpretation to be done?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your job at that company?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I drove a bus at AutoTransport.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you remember about that person, during the time that you worked together?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: (redacted) specific. Her conduct was like that. It didn't really inspire confidence in her as a colleague. That was how she behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You came to that conclusion based on what? Did something happen or is that just your opinion?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, things did happen at AutoTransport. There was disciplinary proceedings that was conducted (redacted)

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I left AutoTransport to go to Rudnik, to the mine, to go to the mine. Then afterwards I met with colleagues that I used to work with - and I still meet with them today - and we talked, and at some point, I mentioned certain colleagues, to see where they were. They told me this person drives for Germany, this persons drives there, the conductors are doing this or that and so on. I started to work at the mine. I worked as a mechanic for a while there, and then after that, I worked there as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. In those conversations that you just mentioned, did you ask your colleagues from your former company (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And later they would mention that she had to appear

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your attitude towards that colleague that we were talking about? Did you like to work with her?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No, not really. Because at some point, somebody said, "If she's taking money, then you would be sharing it." And I never shared money like that with any conductor, if any conductor did such a thing. So I didn't want to work with her any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say anything to that effect to anybody?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokic. I have something else to ask you. In 1992, the investigation centre Omarska was established, the Omarska camp. Did you ever in any capacity spend any time in the investigation centre at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I didn't have any need to do so. I didn't have any need to go there. So that is why I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. That will suffice. After the AutoTransport company where you worked as a driver, you moved to the mine to work?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were working in the Omarska mine, could you please tell us what water did you and your colleagues drink at work?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: The water that we used, it was in taps, came from a tap in the bathrooms, in the toilet. We also had outside taps so that we could wash our footwear, and that water, it was possible to drink it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Honours. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any questions from the other Defence counsel? No? There don't seem to be. Mr. Nikolic? Mr. Jovan Simic, would you like to ask anything? No? Very well. Mr. Waidyaratne, then, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, when did you leave the AutoTransport? Was that in 1985?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: In 1985. I think it was in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After that, you worked in the Omarska mine, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, I worked in the Omarska mine, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you were not in contact with the person whom you referred to as (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Not as a colleague at work, but we would meet on the street. Sometimes we would sit down, have a drink maybe, because we hadn't seen each other for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Can you tell us as to why you left AutoTransport in 1985?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I went to the mine because it was closer to my house and the pay was better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And at the mine, you were a heavy-vehicle driver; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: First I worked as a car mechanic and then I drove heavy vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You have a great knowledge with regard to vehicles and maintenance of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, since I'm a mechanic. I can also drive all types of vehicles, from a regular passenger vehicle to heavy vehicles, and also I am a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, can you tell us as to what a firefighters' IMV is, what does that vehicle mean?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: An IMV firefighters' vehicle was used in case of a fire. It was 1.600 cc.'s, and it's a fire engine. It had water hoses in the back, fire-fighting equipment, which the firefighters used in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What is a vehicle which is a referred to as a Niva PD?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: And it's a Lada Niva. It's a heavy-terrain vehicle, and it was used to go to the actual mine, to the mouth of the mine where it was muddy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Have you driven any of these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jokic, you said that in 1992 -- could you tell us in 1992, in May, as to where you were?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: In May, 1992, I was in Lamovita.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it -- were you attached, were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it the 343 Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it a special unit under the command of Cigo, also known as Momcilo Radanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was your unit?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I was a regular soldier of the 343rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't say right now who the commander of the battalion was. I really don't know his name any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who was your immediate commander? Who was in charge of you when you were in Lamovita, according to you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: We were there on guard duty. For a while, I think it was Nenad Panic but I don't remember exactly. I don't know that guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, in the month of June, what were you assigned to do?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: We were conducting village watch, watches.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you drive a Firefighter IMV on the 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ostoja Trebovac, who was attached to the mine, Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was he the person who issued petrol and gasoline to the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How do you know Mr. Ostoja? What was he in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: He worked on the loader before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you accept petrol or gasoline for a vehicle number Niva PD716-62 on the 9th of June in 1992 from the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What did you do on that day, on the 9th of June, 1992? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I was in Lamovita.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: To take the gasoline or petrol, did you go to the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I did. I took a roundabout road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, have you been to the Omarska mine during the month of June and July?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No. Just once I did go there, when we all went to get petrol. After that I didn't go. So I went because of the petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So that means you have -- in your direct examination you said that you had not been to the Omarska mine; now you say that you have been once. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No. No. You come to the petrol station from the other side, and it's a completely roundabout road to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, have you been to the Omarska mine where the people were detained; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that when you served in the 343rd Motorised Brigade your function was to -- was at Lamovita. What did you do in Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: There were lines there from Lamovita to Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you involved in the action just taken in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was your function exactly? Could you explain it or describe it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: To be a guard in the trenches, on the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, just one matter before I conclude. You spoke about a disciplinary action taken against (redacted) in your direct examination; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know in which year it was or when it was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I think it was maybe in 1979 or 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Before you left the AutoTransport?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you complain? You said that she worked as a conductor in the bus that you drove. Did you complain or did you know specifically of any acts committed (redacted); yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: I know about that particular disciplinary measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Which was in 1979, you say?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes my cross. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, you worked in the Omarska mine. I assume that you know where all the different buildings are, where the administration building is, the hangar. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us where the petrol station is in relation to those buildings, and how do you get to it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: The petrol station, looking from the direction of Omarska towards the mine, is about 150 to 200 metres away from those buildings, and you can reach it from the direction of Gradina, also from the direction of Maricka and from the direction of the main gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which way did you use to get to it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Gradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor. No questions. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just have one that I wanted to clarify. After you left AutoTransport - I don't have it in front of me and maybe I don't remember it correctly - I thought I heard you testify that you would occasionally maybe see (redacted) and sit down and have a cup of coffee or something. Was that right or not?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But it was very brief, perhaps five minutes, because I was in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. In your earlier statement that we got you had said: [As read] "I saw -- after I left Transport, I saw her twice at most, and that in passing on the street. We exchanged greetings and didn't stop to speak." But my basic question is: You told us that you didn't like working with her because you didn't have -- there was no confidence there, and that you told your superiors you didn't want to work with her. And I'm just trying to reconcile that with the fact that if you felt that way about her, that afterwards when you saw her, you would want to sit down and have a cup of coffee with her. Do you want to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Why not? We don't have long memories, so at that moment it didn't matter enough for me not to sit down and have coffee with her. But we didn't discuss work or any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But you, if I'm citing you correctly, after you were both gone -- or after you were gone from AutoTransport, you were -- you thought it tolerable enough so that you were willing to sit down and just chat with her about -- for a couple of minutes if you saw her, occasionally, very occasionally; right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. It's a good answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jokic, I have a couple of questions for you myself. When you first saw (redacted) and your first impressions, you said she was specific, and then you talked about confidence, that you lacked confidence in her. Now, what did you want to say that she had this specific type of appearance?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. She would wear jeans, sometimes she would smoke, so that she looked sort of specific. She never wore dresses or anything like that. She would wear sneakers, she had short hair, she had a sort of man's haircut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why? What do you mean about the smoking business? Why was that unusual?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But do you think that smoking is only for men? Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You had coffee with (redacted), you said five minutes. How many times was that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just once?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And five minutes?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JOKIC
utterances.text: Maybe it wasn't even five minutes, because I was in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Mr. Jokic, we have no further questions for you. We thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal and we wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence. The usher will now accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too for having received me and hearing my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now take a break, after which we shall give the rulings, a 45-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Before the Chamber communicates its decisions, I think that there are two aspects that need to be discussed. The first question is to see how we stand with respect to the reports of Mr. Beatovic -- the report of Mr. Beatovic. Once -- (redacted) said yesterday that there were some negotiations underway between the parties, and I think we ought to be informed of the results of those negotiations. The second question that needs to be discussed beforehand is the situation with respect to the Zigic defence and the appearance of four witnesses who have already been presented by the Prosecution. The Prosecution has not responded to the request and we should like to know what the position is before we render a ruling. I am now going to give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers to bring us up to date with respect to the report of Mr. Beatovic because yesterday, during the hearing, Ms. Susan Somers announced that the parties would be meeting to discuss this issue. So may we have an update and if necessary I can hear Mr. Fila after that. Ms. Somers, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Just before we resumed, I spoke again to both Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Fila, having discussed this initially with Mr. Jovanovic a week ago Thursday. Our suggestion as we relayed - and I don't know whether or not counsel will agree to it - is on the issues which the court in Kunarac felt had relevance pursuant to Rule 101 about sentencing, I think that would be -- I think the Chamber should have that in front of it. A good portion of the report -- and I'm not sure if the Chamber has had a chance -- it's a bit lengthy and a bit wordy but it talks about elements and the criticism leading to a finding of effective irrelevance was that it dealt with a situation of peacetime analysis of crimes, perhaps more one-on-one or in a civilian structure not dealing with rape as a crime in war, which was what the discussion centred around principally in the Beatovic report. That would be -- and I had indicated in our initial response under Rule 94 bis that we thought its relevance as to the crimes alleged under the circumstances of a camp was very -- was at best limited and probably not there at all. If in fact, though, the very nature of the crime had certain sentencing consequences in the former Yugoslavia and because of the requirements of what may be considered -- not mandatorily but what may be considered in sentencing, should that become an issue, I think the Chamber has to have something before it and we cannot produce anything better, frankly, at this point. And therefore, if counsel agrees, on the aspects of sentencing, including aggravating and mitigating, then that which was either testified to or which is contained in the incident report, I think would be appropriate. Again, I don't know how much time the Chamber has had to actually review it but it seems that there is a sufficient amount there that if part of the report were stricken, by agreement, and just the sentencing aspects went in, we would really have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, do you wish to respond and add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect and sympathies towards Ms. Somers, I really don't see how you can adopt a finding only half, half of it, and not adopt the other half, without the Chamber deciding. Now, if Ms. Somers agrees, could I put it in the following way? I have boundless confidence in this Trial Chamber, and you yourselves will be able to decide what you're going to accept from that report and what not, and I say in advance that I will not object to anything you decide to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. As to the other matter in hand: As you know, among the four witnesses who would be called, the Defence -- just one moment, please. I was saying the Zigic Defence will be naming Witness R, and that will be the subject of a separate decision. The Defence counsels of Zigic do not precisely define the reasons for which they wish the three witnesses to -- who have already testified -- and I'm trying to see whether they were protected witnesses or not, but you have the request yourself. And as I was saying, the Prosecutor has not stated his views with regard to that subject, so I should like to hear the Prosecution on that subject. Ms. Susan Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In fact, if I understand, because there has been no separate motion that we have received, but if I understand, it would be from the revised list of witnesses for the accused Zigic which was filed on the 15th of February. There are four names, listed as 20 to 23. None of these witnesses, I am told by my colleagues who were present during the earlier part of the trial, testified. None of them testified for the Prosecution. If the Chamber would like me to go into closed session for just -- a private session for a moment just to make sure that we're citing the same names, because I have no other documents before me, only this revised list. Would it be possible, just for a moment, to make sure we're talking about the same people, literally for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, perhaps we can do something else, and that is to give the floor to the Zigic Defence counsel first. Which of you will be taking the floor? It is Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I feel the need to introduce myself first of all. My name is Miodrag Deretic, a lawyer from Prijedor, and I am on the Defence team of the accused Mr. Zoran Zigic. As far as the question you raised is concerned, we previously requested, while I was not on the team myself, that we adopt the transcript for Witness R, who testified in the Tadic case, in the Tadic trial, with respect to Counts 6 and 7, paragraph 37(C). As to the other three individuals, other three witnesses, we consider, and that is why we put the motion forward, that they can tell this Trial Chamber a great deal with respect to the facts, the facts concerning the accusation of Zoran Zigic and related to the events that took place in the Omarska investigation centre or camp and in Keraterm as well. And in that sense, as my learned colleague of the Prosecution has just said -- that is to say, we submitted a list, a revised list of witnesses - I think this was done on the 16th of February, if I'm not mistaken - and so far we have not heard the Trial Chamber's opinion on that. Unfortunately, I also have to state here and now that on Monday we could submit a third version of these witnesses, and this in view of the fact that everything -- all the things that happened with respect to the Zigic Defence case. I should like to beg the Court's indulgence that our request will be met by the Trial Chamber, the request with respect to the revised list of witnesses that we shall be presenting on Monday, as I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, are matters clearer now? I hope you're looking at the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I am looking at the one from -- it looks like a filing of -- it says the 15th of February, Your Honour. And we responded to the last witness list of the 21st. I think this one may have -- I'm not sure if there was a gap in our response, and if so, we apologise, both to the Chamber and to counsel. Witness R's issue we did address in a motion, a response to their motion, and that was that we would not oppose the introduction of the transcript. We thought that was reasonable. That was combined with a motion, a joint motion with the accused Kos. The other named persons - again, I hope they're the same persons - did not testify for the Prosecution but may testify in another -- in a sister case and may have protected status in that case. However, they have not come in for the Prosecution in its case in chief. There are other names listed that cause us very grave concern, and the Chamber had not addressed them, and they concern accused in other cases. And I think that poses a very great problem in the absence of knowing whether or not counsel for the accused in other cases is aware that these individuals have been listed. And those two names appear, number 18 and 19 on the list that was filed the 15th of February, accused in the Keraterm case. Given the direction in which cross-examination can go, I think there would be very serious ethical considerations if counsel were not aware of it, and I would certainly hope -- I would ask the Chamber for an order giving an assurance that this matter is covered. It would put us in an untenable position and I think it would also cause the Chamber some serious problems. Because of the fact that we did not call the other four civilian witnesses, I think if the Chamber is minded to dispose of the Witness R issue on the transcript, we do not oppose that. And as to the other three, there may be a need for protective measures, and I can only ask if we can check with the Keraterm team and see if this has become an issue, lest there be a conflict in status. But as to us, we did not call them at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I just clarify something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Does that mean that if the Defence wish to call them and the witnesses wish to appear and the protective business is taken care of, then you don't have any objection? I mean, it's not clear to me what your position is. Just those three. I've got R and never mind the accused. Just those three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not sure that the witnesses know they are listed. If in fact they are willing to come in and so represent, then I think it's out of our hands because the measures were brought on their behalf based on what they would have asked for at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So your position basically is you don't have any responsibility except to warn us that somebody should make sure any protective measures are taken care of, but if they -- you don't have any responsibility for producing them for the defence, and if they want to come in on their own and their counsel are all apprised of all of the problems and they come in, you're not making any objection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is as to the accused or as to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, just the three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The three? The three, Your Honour, I think that is the witnesses' call absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that what we can decide here and now with respect to this question of list of witnesses for the accused Zigic is to say that we will wait. If I understand Mr. Deretic correctly, he said that perhaps next Monday he's going to consider another list. Did I understand you correctly, Mr. Deretic, to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that you have understood me absolutely correctly, but if I may, may I add a sentence here? And that is that my learned colleague, Mr. Slobodan Stojanovic, has already talked to the Prosecution with respect to the testimonies of these three witnesses, and that she was against it, and that is why we raised the question. And we would like to have the Trial Chamber make a decision, in view of the fact that our learned colleague of the Prosecution was opposed to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I take a moment? Thank you, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Witness R, if this is about Witness R -- oh, okay. Any other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No. No issues.
